title: U.S. Rule—Making Partial Note Payments before Due Date

questions.prompt: Under the U.S. Rule, a payment is applied first to ___.
Loan $5,000 at 8%. After 3 months, borrower pays $1,000. Interest accrued? (number only, no $)
If interest is $100 and payment is $1,000, how much reduces principal? (number only, no $)

teacherCues: Ask: 'If you make a partial payment on a loan before maturity, should it reduce principal immediately?'
Explain that under the U.S. Rule, interest is paid first.

visuals.title: U.S. Rule Payment Application
visuals.caption: Interest is always settled first; only leftover reduces principal.

notes: Time (T) is the period from the last payment (or loan date) to the current payment date.
If payment is less than accrued interest, principal is not reduced (unusual).
formulaCard.title: U.S. Rule – Interest Calculation
formulaCard.formula: $$I = P \times R \times T$$ $$\text{Principal Reduction} = \text{Payment} - I$$ $$\text{New Principal} = \text{Old Principal} - \text{Principal Reduction}$$

explanation: [[kw:U.S. Rule]] is a method that allows partial payments on a simple interest loan before the due date.
Each payment is applied first to the interest accrued since the last payment (or the loan date), and the rest reduces the principal.
The interest is calculated using the simple interest formula $$I = P \times R \times T$$ on the current principal for the time elapsed.
After the payment, a new principal balance is computed, and interest continues on that new balance.
[[imp:Interest is always paid before principal is reduced.]]

confusionCorner.body: If the payment is less than the accrued interest, the unpaid interest is not added to principal—it remains a separate liability. [[imp:Partial payment must exceed interest to reduce principal.]]
confusionCorner.title: Watch out!

notes: Use ordinary interest (360 days) unless otherwise stated.
Final payment = Remaining principal + interest since last payment.
formulaCard.title: U.S. Rule Step‑by‑Step
formulaCard.formula: $$\text{For each payment:}$$ $$I = \text{Current Principal} \times R \times \frac{\text{Days since last payment}}{360 \text{ (or 365)}}$$ $$\text{Principal Reduction} = \text{Payment} - I$$ $$\text{New Principal} = \text{Old Principal} - \text{Principal Reduction}$$

explanation: When there are multiple partial payments, apply the U.S. Rule sequentially.
For each payment: calculate interest on the current principal from the date of the last payment to the current payment date, subtract interest from payment, reduce principal.
The new principal becomes the base for the next period's interest calculation.
This is repeated until the final payment, which may be for the remaining principal plus final interest.
[[imp:Keep a schedule; do not skip steps.]]

teacherCues: Show a timeline with multiple payments.
Emphasize that after each payment, principal is reset and interest is calculated on the new balance.

formulaCard.formula: $$\text{Exact Days} = \text{End Date Day Number} - \text{Start Date Day Number}$$ $$I = P \times R \times \frac{\text{Exact Days}}{360 \text{ (or 365)}}$$
notes: Day numbers from year‑of‑day table; exclude start date.
Use same denominator (360/365) for all interest calculations within a problem unless told otherwise.
formulaCard.title: U.S. Rule with Dates

explanation: When loan and payment dates are given, count the exact number of days between them, excluding the start date and including the payment date.
Then use the simple interest formula with the appropriate denominator (360 for ordinary, 365 for exact).
Apply the U.S. Rule as before: interest first, then principal reduction.
Continue for subsequent payments, counting days from the previous payment date.
[[imp:Days count is critical; double‑check using a day‑of‑year table or manual month‑by‑month count.]]

discoveryHook.scenario: After several partial payments, the remaining principal is small. The borrower makes one last payment that includes that remaining principal and the interest accrued since the last payment. This final payment closes the loan.

explanation: The last payment under the U.S. Rule must cover any remaining principal and the interest accrued from the last payment date to the payoff date.
Final Payment = Remaining Principal + Interest on that principal for the time since last payment.
If the final payment is made exactly at maturity, it's just the remaining principal (no further interest).
This ensures the loan is fully paid off with no residual balance.
[[imp:Check that the final payment when added to all previous principal reductions equals the original principal.]]

formulaCard.title: Final Payment Calculation
notes: If the final payment is made exactly at maturity, no extra interest is due beyond the last period's interest.
If the final payment is late, additional interest may be calculated.
formulaCard.formula: $$\text{Final Payment} = \text{Remaining Principal} + I_{\text{last period}}$$ $$I_{\text{last period}} = \text{Remaining Principal} \times R \times \frac{\text{Days since last payment}}{360 \text{ (or 365)}}$$

discoveryHook.scenario: A note for $9,000 dated April 1 at 8% ordinary interest receives two partial payments: $4,000 on June 15 and $3,000 on August 20. The blueprint organizes the count of days, interest calculations, and principal reductions.

notes: Keep a schedule with dates, days, interest, and principal.
Final payment = remaining P + last interest.
formulaCard.title: U.S. Rule Blueprint
formulaCard.formula: $$\text{For each payment: } I = \text{Current P} \times R \times \frac{\text{Days}}{360 \text{ (or 365)}}$$ $$\text{Reduction} = \text{Payment} - I$$ $$\text{New P} = \text{Old P} - \text{Reduction}$$

explanation: Apply the three‑step blueprint to U.S. Rule problems:
1. Understand: identify original principal, rate, ordinary/exact, loan date, payment dates and amounts.
2. Solve: for each payment, count days from previous payment (or loan date), calculate interest, reduce principal, repeat.
3. Conclude: verify that the sum of principal reductions equals the original principal and that the final payment is consistent.
A table or schedule helps keep track.
